correctness.rationale: Two adjacent columns form K4, so any adjacent occupancies summing to at least three are impossible. Conversely, with adjacent sums at most two, double columns induce isolated edges and runs of singleton columns induce paths, for any choices of rows. An empty column is blocked exactly by an adjacent double, and a singleton exactly by an adjacent singleton; unavailable end neighbors do not count. For p double, q singleton and r empty columns, r≤2p, q≠1, and n≤s+p for s=2p+q. If s≤2k then n≤3k; at s=2k+1 one has odd q≥3, so p≤k−1 and still n≤3k. This implies s≥2ceil(n/3). The three residue constructions separate all double columns by zeros and cover all zeros by adjacent doubles, with exactly ceil(n/3) doubles. They include n=1 and 2. value.rationale: This determines the lower bipartite number for the smallest nontrivial king-strip width, including boundaries, and gives a local test for all inclusion-maximal sets. The lower bound accounts for singleton columns rather than assuming an optimal solution is an ordinary dominating construction. Both the precise minimum and the occupancy test are useful for comparing nearby strip invariants and for higher-width work.
